title: Chess Elevator
reviewNotes: All 38 board diagrams/captions reviewed; native image31 at 112 seconds confirms the complete ten-piece later root after Kc4. Selected final elevator stage Rb4+/Kxc3/Bd2 mate is proved against the sole legal defense. The white c3 pawn protects b4, then its capture places Black where Kd1 can support the bishop mate. Earlier queen/bishop sacrifices and elevator checks remain unverified; this is explicitly a short mating-net lesson, not the full composition.
transcript: White can promote to a new queen, but why is this a brilliant move? Well, as it turns out, the queen is hanging. The black queen can simply capture it seemingly for free. But, this is no regular chess position, and [music] despite only having two bishops and one rook against the queen and the bishop, white is completely winning thanks to an incredible sequence. And that sequence continues with another majestic sacrifice. Bishop to D5, attacking the queen, but of course leaving the bishop to hang. First of all, the queen has to take because if it moves, for example, to A7, now after the very precise bishop to F4, white is defending the C pawn and preparing a rook to B8, which would lead to a checkmate. And there is simply no way to prevent the idea, so white would win. But, black is not that naive, and of course, after bishop to D5, he's just going to take the free bishop. After all, rook to B8 is not a checkmate. The king can simply take the pawn. Right? Well, yes. After rook to B8, a mysterious move, the king can take the pawn, and most of us would stop our calculation here, realize that we have a rook for a queen, and that we are lost. But, fools will resign, and we have to follow the checks. And indeed, bishop to F4 keeps the game going. And although we might not know for sure that we're going to be able to win, we have to try. Now, of course, this defends the rook with an X-ray, and the only move for the king is to go to C6. Now, white only has two checks. One of them is just a full rook blunder, and the other one lands us in a similar situation where the king yet again only has one option, to capture the other pawn. And I think you're starting to see where I'm going with this. This position is an extremely unique chess elevator. We keep forcing the king to walk up the board, and we use the pawn to give more checks with the rook. And the black pieces take away the only other square that the king could use to escape. And finally, once the king collects the C pawn, this time our king is defending the C2 square, which means that bishop D2 is a beautiful checkmate.
